title: Developer tools: network, console and elements

videos.script: Ten lessons of things you were asked to take on trust. Here is where you stop taking them on trust. {{trust}} Every single thing this course has described is visible in a panel that came with your browser. Not a simulation of it — the actual requests, the actual headers, the actual tree, the actual milliseconds. {{visible}} The cookies of lesson seven, with their attributes as columns. The status codes of lesson six, in a list. The DNS and the connection and the wait of lesson three, as four separate bars you can read apart. The layout and the paint of lesson ten, with durations. {{list}} All of it, on any site, including sites you did not build. Which is the part worth sitting with: you can open this on anything and see how it was made. {{any-site}} This lesson is four panels and one habit. The habit is the valuable half. {{habit}} It is: look before guessing. Almost every argument about a slow site, a wrong page or a missing cookie is settled by opening this and reading one number — and almost nobody opens it, because nobody showed them which number. {{look-first}} That is what the rest of this lesson is for. {{title}}

Two real faults, found from nothing, with the panel you have just learned. First one. A shop page that takes six seconds, on a connection that is not slow. {{fault-one}} Open the network panel and reload. Sort by time. {{sort}} There it is, at the top: one request, five and a half seconds, and everything else is under two hundred milliseconds. So the page is not slow — one thing in it is. {{one-thing}} Click it. Look at the timing breakdown: the connection took nine milliseconds and the waiting took five and a half seconds. That separates the network from the server, and this is the server. {{waiting}} And look at the name. It is not on this site. It is a third-party script, on a host that is having a bad afternoon, and it was written without async — so lesson ten's parser is stopped behind somebody else's outage. {{third-party}} One attribute fixes the page. Nothing about the site was wrong. {{fix-one}} Second fault, and a different shape. A form that says it saved and did not. {{fault-two}} Console first. No errors — which is itself information, because it means nothing threw. {{no-errors}} Network. There is the request, and the status is 200. So the client thinks it worked. {{two-hundred}} Open the response. And there it is: a body that says error, validation failed, under a 200. {{lie}} That is lesson six's most expensive mistake, seen from the outside: the number said success, so nothing in between — no retry, no monitoring, no cache — knew otherwise. Including the code that showed the visitor a confirmation. {{diagnosis}} Neither of those needed a debugger, a log, or access to the server. Both were four clicks in a panel that was already open. {{close}}
